content: The umbilical cord is a vital structure composed of blood vessels and connective tissue that connects the fetus to the placenta during pregnancy. After birth, the umbilical cord is cut, symbolically and physically separating the newborn from the mother. Infection of the umbilical cord stump, known as omphalitis, can occur, and bacterial spread through the umbilical vessels may lead to neonatal sepsis, a condition associated with significant morbidity and mortality, particularly in developing countries. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effects of applying antimicrobial agents to the umbilical cord compared to routine or dry cord care in preventing neonatal morbidity and mortality in both hospital and community settings. A comprehensive search of multiple databases identified 77 trials, of which 34 were included in the review, involving a total of 69,338 newborns. The studies were conducted in both developed and developing countries, with data from community and hospital settings analyzed separately. In community settings, three large cluster-randomized trials accounted for 78% of the total participants in the review. Chlorhexidine was the only antiseptic studied in these settings. These trials reported a 23% reduction in all-cause neonatal mortality in the chlorhexidine group compared to the control group (risk ratio [RR] 0.77, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.63 to 0.94). Chlorhexidine also reduced the incidence of omphalitis by 27% to 56%, depending on the severity of the infection. However, the use of chlorhexidine increased the time for the umbilical cord to separate by an average of 1.7 days compared to dry cord care (mean difference [MD] 1.75 days, 95% CI 0.44 to 3.05). Washing the umbilical cord with soap and water did not provide any additional benefit over dry cord care in community settings. In hospital settings, the majority of studies had small sample sizes, and no data were reported on neonatal mortality or tetanus. No antiseptic was found to be superior to dry cord care in reducing the incidence of omphalitis. However, the application of triple dye reduced bacterial colonization with Staphylococcus aureus compared to dry cord care (RR 0.15, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.22) or alcohol application (RR 0.45, 95% CI 0.25 to 0.80). Alcohol application was effective in reducing colonization with Enterococcus coli compared to dry cord care (RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.58 to 0.92). In contrast, triple dye increased the risk of colonization with Enterococcus coli compared to alcohol (RR 3.44, 95% CI 2.10 to 5.64). Both alcohol and triple dye significantly increased the time for cord separation compared to dry cord care, with alcohol delaying separation by an average of 1.76 days (MD 1.76 days, 95% CI 0.03 to 3.48) and triple dye by 4.10 days (MD 4.10 days, 95% CI 3.07 to 5.13). The authors concluded that there is strong evidence supporting the use of chlorhexidine for umbilical cord care in community and primary care settings in developing countries, as it reduces neonatal mortality and omphalitis. While chlorhexidine may prolong cord separation time, there is no evidence to suggest it increases the risk of subsequent morbidity or infection. In contrast, there is insufficient evidence to recommend the use of antiseptics over dry cord care in hospital settings in developed countries.
